title: Glomerular Filtration and Renal Blood Flow

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: At rest, roughly what share of cardiac output do an adult human's two kidneys receive, and how much of its oxygen do they extract?
cards.back: About a quarter of cardiac output, and they extract little of its oxygen: the flow far exceeds what kidney cells need, because it supplies a filter.
cards.quote: receive about a quarter of the blood the heart pumps, and they extract little of its oxygen

cards.front: In an adult at rest the glomeruli filter about {{c1::125 mL of plasma a minute}}, about 180 L a day.
cards.back: The tubules return all but 1 to 2 L of it.
cards.quote: In an adult at rest the glomeruli filter about 125 mL of plasma a minute, about 180 L a day

cards.front: Plasma filters wherever the hydrostatic push out of the glomerular capillary beats the oncotic pull. What two things therefore set GFR?
cards.back: How high the push is (P_GC less Bowman's-space pressure), and how much plasma flows through, because faster flow slows the concentrating of the protein left behind.
cards.quote: So GFR depends on two things: how high that pressure is, and how much plasma flows through, which slows the concentrating of the protein.

cards.front: Why does the afferent arteriole move glomerular pressure and plasma flow the same way, while the efferent arteriole moves them opposite ways?
cards.back: Total arteriolar resistance sets the flow; the efferent share of that resistance sets P_GC. Afferent constriction raises total and lowers efferent share; efferent constriction raises both.
cards.why: So afferent constriction lowers flow and P_GC together, while efferent constriction lowers flow but raises P_GC.
cards.quote: Their total resistance sets the flow. The share of that resistance in the efferent arteriole, downstream of the glomerulus, sets the pressure.

cards.front: Name the three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier, from capillary lumen to Bowman's space.
cards.back: Fenestrated endothelium coated with a negatively charged glycocalyx; the basement membrane; podocyte foot processes, with the gaps between them bridged by the slit diaphragm.
cards.quote: Podocytes: cells that wrap the capillary in foot processes, with the gaps between them bridged by the slit diaphragm.
cards.section: What passes and what stays

cards.front: What human genetic evidence implicates the podocyte slit diaphragm in holding plasma protein back?
cards.back: NPHS1 (nephrin) mutations cause congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type; NPHS2 (podocin) mutations segregate with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Both give heavy protein loss in urine.
cards.quote: Human genetics implicates the slit diaphragm: NPHS1 mutations (nephrin) cause congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type
cards.section: What passes and what stays

cards.front: Why does hydrostatic pressure barely fall along a glomerular capillary, unlike most systemic capillaries?
cards.back: The glomerular capillary sits between two resistances, the afferent and efferent arterioles, so the pressure drop happens across the arterioles rather than along the capillary.
cards.quote: the glomerular capillary sits between two resistances, the afferent and efferent arterioles, so its hydrostatic pressure barely falls along its length
cards.section: Push against pull along one capillary

cards.front: Name the four Starling forces across the glomerular capillary and say which favour filtration and which oppose it.
cards.back: Favour: capillary hydrostatic pressure (P_GC) and Bowman's-space oncotic pressure (π_BS). Oppose: Bowman's-space hydrostatic pressure (P_BS) and capillary oncotic pressure (π_GC).
cards.why: π_BS is normally near zero, because almost no protein gets through the filter.
cards.quote: These are the four Starling forces: two favour filtration (P_GC and π_BS) and two oppose it (P_BS and π_GC).
cards.section: Push against pull along one capillary

cards.front: Illustrative glomerular capillary: P_GC 55 mmHg throughout, P_BS 15 mmHg, π_GC entering 25 mmHg, π_BS 0. If 18% of the plasma filters, and oncotic pressure were proportional to protein concentration, what is net filtration pressure at the afferent and efferent ends?
cards.back: Afferent: 55 − 15 − 25 = +15 mmHg. Protein is concentrated 1 / (1 − 0.18) = 1.22-fold, so efferent π_GC = 30.5 mmHg and net pressure = +9.5 mmHg.
cards.why: Real oncotic pressure rises faster than linearly with concentration, so this underestimates efferent π_GC.
cards.quote: If 18% of the plasma filters out, the remaining 82% holds the same protein
cards.section: Push against pull along one capillary

cards.front: What is filtration pressure equilibrium in a glomerular capillary?
cards.back: The point where the rising oncotic pull of concentrated plasma protein meets the hydrostatic push before the efferent end. Beyond that point nothing filters.
cards.quote: If enough water leaves, the pull can rise to meet the push before the efferent end.
cards.section: Push against pull along one capillary

cards.front: A glomerular capillary reaches filtration pressure equilibrium partway along. Plasma flow through it rises while the pressures stay the same. Where is equilibrium reached now, and what happens to single-nephron GFR?
cards.back: Later along the capillary, so SNGFR rises. Each millilitre of filtrate is drawn from more plasma, so protein concentrates more slowly and more of the capillary keeps filtering.
cards.why: With equilibrium, SNGFR depends strongly on plasma flow; without it, flow still matters, only less.
cards.quote: Each millilitre of filtrate is drawn from more plasma, so the protein concentrates more slowly.
cards.section: Push against pull along one capillary

cards.front: Two-resistor model of the glomerulus: arterial pressure 100 mmHg, venous 10 mmHg, afferent and efferent resistance 1 unit each. Find plasma flow and P_GC, then recompute after doubling efferent resistance to 2 units.
cards.back: Baseline: flow = 90 / 2 = 45 units; P_GC = 10 + 90 × 1/2 = 55 mmHg. Efferent doubled: flow = 90 / 3 = 30 (down a third); P_GC = 10 + 90 × 2/3 = 70 mmHg.
cards.why: Total resistance sets flow; the efferent share of resistance sets P_GC above venous pressure.
cards.quote: Efferent doubled: total resistance 3, so flow = 90 / 3 = 30, down by a third.
cards.section: Two taps on one hose: the afferent and efferent arterioles

cards.front: In the same two-resistor model (100 and 10 mmHg, both arterioles 1 unit), the afferent resistance doubles instead. With P_BS 15 mmHg and entering π_GC 25 mmHg, what is net filtration pressure at the afferent end?
cards.back: Flow = 90 / 3 = 30; efferent share 1/3, so P_GC = 10 + 90 × 1/3 = 40 mmHg. Net pressure = 40 − 15 − 25 = 0: filtration stops.
cards.why: Combines the resistor rule with the Starling balance: GFR depends steeply on P_GC.
cards.quote: a hard afferent squeeze can stop filtration, which shows how steeply GFR depends on P_GC
cards.section: Two taps on one hose: the afferent and efferent arterioles

cards.front: The filtration fraction (FF) is the share of plasma flow that is filtered, {{c1::GFR / RPF}}.
cards.quote: The filtration fraction (FF) is the share of plasma flow that is filtered, GFR / RPF.
cards.section: From pressure and flow to GFR

cards.front: Why does afferent arteriolar constriction lower GFR, and what happens to filtration fraction?
cards.back: P_GC and plasma flow fall together: two losses, so GFR falls. The textbook shortcut keeps FF unchanged, but with lower P_GC the oncotic pull catches up sooner, so FF tends to fall.
cards.quote: Afferent constriction lowers pressure and flow together: two losses, so GFR falls.
cards.section: From pressure and flow to GFR

cards.front: Why can efferent arteriolar constriction raise GFR when mild but lower it when severe?
cards.back: Mild: the rise in P_GC wins, so GFR rises slightly. Severe: P_GC levels off because it can never exceed arterial pressure, while flow keeps falling and protein concentrates sooner, so GFR falls.
cards.why: FF rises throughout, because a larger share of the plasma is filtered.
cards.quote: With a hard squeeze the pressure gain levels off, because P_GC can never exceed arterial pressure, while flow keeps falling, so GFR falls.
cards.section: From pressure and flow to GFR

cards.front: A patient with poorly perfused kidneys, who depends on angiotensin II, starts an ACE inhibitor. What happens to glomerular capillary pressure and GFR, and why?
cards.back: Both fall, most when perfusion pressure is already low. Losing angiotensin II relaxes the efferent arteriole most, so the efferent share of resistance falls and P_GC falls.
cards.why: An ARB does the same, which is one reason clinicians check plasma creatinine after starting either drug.
cards.quote: Losing angiotensin II relaxes the efferent arteriole most.
cards.section: Two drugs as tests of the rule

cards.front: A patient with high circulating angiotensin II takes an NSAID. Predict the effect on GFR and give the reason.
cards.back: GFR can fall. Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole; NSAIDs block their synthesis, so the afferent arteriole can constrict, most when angiotensin II and other constrictors are already high.
cards.quote: NSAIDs block their synthesis, so the afferent arteriole can constrict and GFR can fall
cards.section: Two drugs as tests of the rule

cards.front: A poorly perfused patient whose GFR depends on angiotensin II takes both an ACE inhibitor and an NSAID. Using the two-resistor rule, predict P_GC and GFR compared with either drug alone.
cards.back: Both are likely to fall further than with either drug alone. The NSAID lets the afferent arteriole constrict while the ACE inhibitor relaxes the efferent arteriole, so the efferent share of resistance falls from both ends.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the efferent share of total resistance sets P_GC.
cards.quote: Its share of the resistance falls, so P_GC and GFR fall, most when perfusion pressure is already low.
cards.section: Two drugs as tests of the rule

cards.front: Two-resistor glomerulus, venous pressure 10 mmHg, both arterioles 1 unit. Arterial pressure rises from 100 to 130 mmHg. What are the new flow and P_GC, and what afferent resistance restores flow 45 and P_GC 55 mmHg?
cards.back: Unadjusted: flow = 120 / 2 = 60; P_GC = 10 + 120 / 2 = 70 mmHg. Afferent 5/3 unit: total 8/3, flow = 120 × 3/8 = 45; efferent share 3/8, P_GC = 10 + 120 × 3/8 = 55 mmHg.
cards.quote: Raise the afferent resistance to 5/3 of a unit.
cards.section: Why the controls act upstream

cards.front: Why must the controls that buffer arterial pressure changes act on the afferent rather than the efferent arteriole?
cards.back: Only the afferent arteriole can return both flow and P_GC at once. Relaxing the efferent arteriole (to 0.6 unit after a rise to 130 mmHg) restores P_GC to 55 mmHg but raises flow to 75.
cards.quote: Only the afferent arteriole can cancel a change in arterial pressure on both at once.
cards.section: Why the controls act upstream

cards.front: What must be true of a substance for its clearance (U × V / P) to equal GFR?
cards.back: It must be freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so U × V = GFR × P. Inulin behaves this way.
cards.quote: If a substance is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, everything filtered reaches the urine
cards.section: Measuring it in a person: clearance

cards.front: Why does PAH clearance measure renal plasma flow, and why is it called effective renal plasma flow (ERPF)?
cards.back: PAH is filtered and also secreted, so one pass removes roughly 90% of it from arterial blood. Because that extraction is incomplete, PAH clearance slightly underestimates plasma flow.
cards.quote: Because extraction is incomplete, PAH clearance slightly underestimates plasma flow and is called effective renal plasma flow (ERPF).
cards.section: Measuring it in a person: clearance

cards.front: Adult at rest, steady state: urine inulin 30 mg per mL, urine flow 0.8 mL per min, plasma inulin 0.20 mg per mL. What is GFR per minute and per day?
cards.back: GFR = inulin clearance = 30 × 0.8 / 0.20 = 120 mL per min; × 1,440 min = about 173 L per day.
cards.quote: Inulin behaves this way, so inulin clearance is GFR.
cards.section: Measuring it in a person: clearance

cards.front: Adult at rest: urine PAH 13 mg per mL, urine flow 1.0 mL per min, plasma PAH 0.020 mg per mL, PAH extraction 0.90, hematocrit 0.45, GFR 125 mL per min. Find ERPF, true RPF, RBF and filtration fraction.
cards.quote: RBF = 694 / 0.55 = about 1,260 mL per min, about 25% of cardiac output.
cards.section: Worked problem: filtration, flow and a drifting marker

cards.front: Creatinine production is constant at 1.0 mg per min, and creatinine is treated as filtered only. GFR falls from 125 to 50 mL per min. What is plasma creatinine before and at the new steady state?
cards.back: At steady state excretion = production, so P_cr = production / GFR. Before: 1.0 / 125 = 0.008 mg per mL = 0.8 mg per dL. After: 1.0 / 50 = 0.02 mg per mL = 2.0 mg per dL.
cards.why: Excretion falls first, and creatinine accumulates over days until excretion again matches production.
cards.quote: At steady state excretion equals production, so P_cr = 1.0 / 125 = 0.008 mg per mL = 0.8 mg per dL.
cards.section: Worked problem: filtration, flow and a drifting marker

cards.front: Why does creatinine clearance overestimate GFR?
cards.back: Proximal tubule cells secrete creatinine through transporters, so more reaches the urine than was filtered and clearance exceeds GFR.
cards.quote: But proximal tubule cells also secrete creatinine through transporters, so creatinine clearance exceeds GFR
cards.section: Worked problem: filtration, flow and a drifting marker

cards.front: A patient starts cobicistat, which blocks the proximal tubule transporters that secrete creatinine. Predict plasma creatinine and inulin clearance.
cards.back: Plasma creatinine rises, but GFR (inulin clearance) is unchanged. Less creatinine is secreted, so it accumulates until filtration alone excretes production.
cards.quote: a drug that blocks those transporters, such as cobicistat, raises plasma creatinine without changing GFR.
cards.section: Worked problem: filtration, flow and a drifting marker

cards.front: In mammals RBF and GFR stay nearly constant over renal perfusion pressures of about {{c1::80 to 180 mmHg}}: autoregulation.
cards.back: Mainly by the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback, both acting mainly on the afferent arteriole.
cards.quote: In mammals RBF and GFR stay nearly constant over renal perfusion pressures of about 80 to 180 mmHg: autoregulation.
cards.section: Holding GFR steady: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.front: How does the myogenic response of the afferent arteriole oppose a rise in perfusion pressure?
cards.back: Stretch of arteriolar smooth muscle depolarizes it, cytosolic calcium rises and the muscle contracts, raising afferent resistance. The stretch sensor is still debated.
cards.quote: In the myogenic response, stretch of arteriolar smooth muscle depolarizes it, cytosolic calcium rises and it contracts.
cards.section: Holding GFR steady: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.front: What and where is the macula densa?
cards.back: A plaque of cells at the end of the thick ascending limb, where each tubule touches its own glomerulus. It senses NaCl, which enters through NKCC2.
cards.quote: a plaque of cells at the end of the thick ascending limb, where each tubule touches its own glomerulus
cards.section: Holding GFR steady: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.front: Trace tubuloglomerular feedback from a rise in NaCl delivery to the macula densa to a fall in single-nephron GFR.
cards.back: NaCl enters macula densa cells via NKCC2; they release ATP; adenosine formed from it acts on Gi-coupled A1 receptors; the afferent arteriole constricts; P_GC and SNGFR fall.
cards.quote: Adenosine formed from it constricts the afferent arteriole through adenosine A1 receptors
cards.section: Holding GFR steady: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.front: NaCl delivery to the macula densa falls. Predict the response of the afferent arteriole and of the granular cells in its wall.
cards.back: The afferent arteriole dilates, raising P_GC and GFR, and the granular cells release renin.
cards.quote: less NaCl dilates it, and granular cells, the renin-secreting cells in the arteriole wall, release renin.
cards.section: Holding GFR steady: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.front: A loop diuretic blocks NKCC2. Predict how tubuloglomerular feedback responds when NaCl delivery to the macula densa then rises.
cards.back: The feedback constriction is blunted: less NaCl enters macula densa cells, so the signal and the constriction are blunted, and the afferent arteriole does not constrict as it normally would.
cards.why: Rests on the stated rule that the macula densa senses NaCl through NKCC2, the loop-diuretic target.
cards.quote: NaCl enters macula densa cells through NKCC2, the cotransporter that loop diuretics block.
cards.section: Holding GFR steady: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.front: Design a micropuncture test, in wild-type and adenosine A1 receptor knockout mice, of whether A1 receptors carry the tubuloglomerular feedback signal. What result supports it?
cards.back: Perfuse the loop of Henle at 0 then 30 nl per min and record proximal stop-flow pressure, which follows P_GC. It should fall in wild type only. Observed: 6.8 versus 0.4 mmHg.
cards.why: Baseline GFR did not differ, so the data do not show feedback sets resting GFR, and a lifelong knockout may compensate developmentally.
cards.quote: If A1 receptors carry the signal, it should fall in wild type only.
cards.section: Holding GFR steady: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.front: How does high plasma glucose in early diabetes cause glomerular hyperfiltration?
cards.back: More glucose is filtered, and the proximal tubule reabsorbs more of it with sodium through SGLT2. In the feedback account, less NaCl reaches the macula densa, the afferent arteriole dilates, and P_GC and GFR rise.
cards.quote: Less NaCl reaches the macula densa, the afferent arteriole dilates, and P_GC and GFR rise: hyperfiltration.
cards.section: Holding GFR steady: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.front: A person with diabetic hyperfiltration starts an SGLT2 inhibitor. Predict GFR and explain it through the macula densa.
cards.back: GFR falls (in the high-GFR group). In the feedback account, less proximal sodium reabsorption sends more NaCl to the macula densa; feedback constricts the afferent arteriole, lowering P_GC.
cards.quote: More NaCl reaches the macula densa, feedback constricts the afferent arteriole, and P_GC and SNGFR fall.
cards.section: Holding GFR steady: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.front: In the high-GFR group of adults with type 1 diabetes under clamped glycemia, an SGLT2 inhibitor lowered inulin clearance and ERPF and raised renal vascular resistance. Why can these data not show which arteriole changed, and what kind of experiment can?
cards.back: Clearances give only whole-kidney flow and resistance, and the study had no control arm. Vessel diameters can: in diabetic rats, luseogliflozin reduced afferent dilation without changing efferent diameter, and an A1 antagonist blocked it.
cards.quote: That study had no control arm, and clearances cannot say which arteriole changed.
cards.section: Holding GFR steady: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

cards.front: Drug A lowers both inulin clearance and PAH clearance, with PAH extraction unchanged. Which single-arteriole changes fit, and how does filtration fraction tell them apart?
cards.back: Afferent constriction or hard efferent constriction. FF stays the same or falls with afferent constriction, and rises with hard efferent constriction, where plasma flow falls much more than GFR.
cards.why: Check extraction with a renal vein sample: a drug that blocks PAH secretion lowers its clearance without lowering flow.
cards.quote: FF tells the two single-arteriole changes apart: it stays the same or falls with afferent constriction, and rises with hard efferent constriction
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Drug B lowers inulin clearance while raising PAH clearance. Which arteriole change fits, and which way does filtration fraction move?
cards.back: Efferent dilation: lower P_GC with higher plasma flow. GFR falls while RPF rises, so FF falls.
cards.quote: That is what lower P_GC with higher flow looks like, so efferent dilation fits, and FF fell.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Drug C lowers GFR with PAH clearance unchanged. List three explanations and the measurements, in an animal micropuncture preparation, that tell them apart.
cards.back: Lower Kf; raised Bowman's-space pressure (tubule blockage); or afferent constriction with matched efferent dilation. Low P_GC marks the paired arteriole change; then raised tubule pressure marks blockage, not a Kf fall.
cards.quote: P_GC separates the paired arteriole change (P_GC lower) from the other two (P_GC about unchanged).
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What does the glomerular filtration coefficient, Kf, represent, and what two changes would lower it?
cards.back: The filter itself: GFR per unit of mean net filtration pressure. Less filtering area or a less permeable capillary wall lowers it.
cards.quote: It could lower Kf (less filtering area or a less permeable wall), raise Bowman's-space pressure (for example by blocking tubules)
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Contrast the internal and external urethral sphincters in muscle type and control.
cards.back: Internal: smooth muscle at the bladder neck, not under voluntary control. External: voluntary skeletal muscle, kept contracted during storage by the pudendal nerve.
cards.quote: the external urethral sphincter is voluntary skeletal muscle
cards.section: Where the filtrate goes: kidney, ureter and bladder

cards.front: During bladder storage, how does sympathetic outflow in the hypogastric nerve act on the detrusor and the bladder neck?
cards.back: It relaxes the detrusor through beta-3 adrenoceptors and contracts the bladder neck through alpha-1 adrenoceptors.
cards.quote: sympathetic fibres in the hypogastric nerve relax the detrusor through beta-3 adrenoceptors and contract the bladder neck through alpha-1 adrenoceptors
cards.section: Where the filtrate goes: kidney, ureter and bladder

cards.front: In the voiding reflex, what transmitter and receptor contract the detrusor, and what happens to the sphincters?
cards.back: Postganglionic neurons driven by sacral pelvic nerve fibres release acetylcholine, acting on muscarinic M3 receptors. Sympathetic and pudendal outflow are inhibited, so both sphincters relax.
cards.why: The reflex runs through the periaqueductal gray and the pontine micturition centre (Barrington's nucleus).
cards.quote: these postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine, which contracts the detrusor through muscarinic M3 receptors
cards.section: Where the filtrate goes: kidney, ureter and bladder
